cards.body: Every website lives on a computer called a server. Your browser asks the server for the page, the server sends it back, and your browser draws it on your screen. That request-and-response dance is the entire web.
cards.title: The web in 30 seconds

cards.body: A server is just a regular computer that stays on all the time, waiting for requests. When you type a URL and hit enter, your browser sends a request across the internet, and the server replies with files: text, images, and code.
cards.title: Servers never sleep

cards.body: Request goes out, response comes back. Every click, every form you submit, every page you load follows this rhythm. Once you see it, the web stops feeling like magic.

This very lesson did it: your browser asked a server for this page, the server sent back text and code, and your browser turned it into the screen you're reading right now. You just completed a round trip.

choices: Waits for requests and sends back files
cards.explain: The server's job is simple: sit there, wait for a browser to ask for something, and send the files back. Your browser does all the drawing.
cards.q: What does a web server do?

choices: It sends a request to a server
questions.explain: Nothing appears until the browser asks. The request always comes first, then the server responds, then the page renders.
questions.q: Your browser wants to show you a website. What happens first?

questions.explain: Websites live on servers. Your browser just borrows a copy for a little while to show you.
questions.q: Where does a website actually live?

choices: Turns the code into a visible page
questions.explain: The browser's whole job is rendering: translating HTML, CSS, and code into the page you see and click.
questions.q: What does your browser do with the server's response?

choices: Clicking a link to load a new page
Reading text already on your screen
questions.explain: Clicking a link asks the server for something new — that's a request. Reading what's already loaded needs no trip to the server.
questions.q: Which of these counts as a request?

choices: The page loads from memory forever
Your browser builds the page itself
questions.explain: No server, no response, no page. Your browser can't invent a website it was never sent.
questions.q: The server is down. What happens when you visit the site?

flashcards.back: An always-on computer that stores websites and sends them to browsers when asked.
The app you browse with (Chrome, Safari, Firefox). It requests pages and turns code into what you see.
A message your browser sends to a server, asking for a page or a file.
The server's reply: the files your browser needs to display the page.

cards.body: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the skeleton of every webpage. It describes what is on the page: headings, paragraphs, images, links, buttons. No HTML, no page — everything else is decoration.
cards.title: HTML gives pages bones

cards.body: If HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the clothes, the haircut, and the attitude. It controls colors, fonts, spacing, and layout. Same HTML with different CSS can look like a completely different website.
cards.title: CSS is the wardrobe

cards.body: A CSS rule points at HTML with a selector. In p { color: red; }, the p selects every paragraph and the rule turns their text red. Selector picks the target, declaration changes it.
cards.title: Selectors pick their targets

cards.body: A URL is an address for the web. https:// is the protocol (how to get there), example.com is the domain (which building), and /about is the path (which room). Every part has a job.
cards.title: URLs are street addresses

cards.body: Read a URL left to right: https://shop.example.com/shoes means a secure connection, to example.com, the shop section, the shoes page. You'll never get lost in a link again.

cards.explain: CSS is purely about presentation: colors, fonts, spacing, layout. Content comes from HTML, files live on servers.

choices: How it looks: colors, fonts, layout
The text content on the page
questions.explain: CSS only touches presentation. The words and structure (HTML) and the hosting (server) are untouched.
questions.q: A page's HTML stays the same but you swap its CSS. What changes?

choices: Sets the text color to red
questions.explain: Declarations live inside the curly braces and change one property — here, the text color of whatever the selector picked.
questions.q: What does the declaration color: red do?

choices: The path: a specific page on the site
questions.explain: Everything after the domain is the path — it points to a specific page or resource on that site.

choices: It encrypts the connection so others can't snoop
It makes pages load ten times faster
questions.explain: The s stands for secure: https encrypts traffic between you and the server, which matters for logins and payments.
questions.q: Why does https matter instead of plain http?

questions.explain: The selector (like p or .title) picks the targets. The declaration block says what to change about them.
questions.q: Which part of a CSS rule chooses the elements to style?

flashcards.back: The selector — it picks which HTML elements the rule applies to.
flashcards.front: In p { color: red; }, what is p?

flashcards.back: A secure, encrypted connection between your browser and the server.
flashcards.front: What does https:// at the start of a URL mean?

flashcards.back: The domain — the human-readable address of the website.
